title: Heme & Endo Exam 3 Hub
examInfo: Exam 3: 35 multiple-choice questions on new material only: Dr. Taylor's Lecture A and L17-L22. Nothing from Exam 1 or Exam 2's lectures.
Friday, November 20, 8:00-9:30 am (the dental students' sitting; optometry sits at 10:00).
In person, Volker Hall Lecture Room B, on Canvas with LockDown Browser, as for Exams 1 and 2.

A Dental endocrinology clinical application (Dr. Taylor), L17 Pregnancy and lactation (Dr. Madison), L18 Estrogens and androgens (Dr. Fasinu), L19 Introduction to hematology (Dr. Herr), L20 Lymphomas and leukemias (Dr. Borak), L21 and L22 Pathology of the male and female reproductive systems (Dr. Dal Zotto).

There's no in-class review for Exam 3: Dr. Herr gave a study guide instead (November 17), with the points to focus on and the key terms for L17 to L22. Everything on it is a High Likelihood question in this hub, and its lists open each lecture's Exam Hints.
Dr. Taylor's lecture was taught November 6 but left off Exam 2 (Dr. Herr said he forgot it), so it moved to Exam 3 with everything the Exam 2 hub had for it.

Of the 35: Lecture A (Clinical application) 3, L17 Pregnancy and lactation 4, L18 Estrogens and androgens 6, L19 Introduction to hematology 8, L20 Lymphomas and leukemias 6, L21 Male reproductive pathology 4 and L22 Female reproductive pathology 4. The mock follows the same counts.
Quiz 4 is due Thursday, November 19, at 11:59 pm. This hub uses nothing from the quizzes or the take-home.

lectures.title: Male Reproductive and Lower Urinary Tract Pathology

likelyTopics.t: Hypoglycemia in the chair: the signs, a finger-stick (some CGMs stop reading at a floor), straight glucose rather than table sugar, a slow response on a GLP-1 drug, glucagon IM or subcutaneously if oral glucose fails

Before treating a diabetic: HbA1c above 7 is poorly controlled (implant failure, periodontal disease), confirm the meal and medication, morning appointments; Dr. Taylor's metformin with a skipped breakfast; pack-years
Hyperthyroidism and Graves disease (his first case): epinephrine caution, and thyroid storm (fever, pulse 140 or more; call 911)
Addison disease (his third case): oral pigment from high ACTH, adrenal crisis triggers and signs, extra corticosteroid after a big procedure; Cushing syndrome and long-term steroids
Hyperparathyroidism on the radiograph (lost lamina dura, radiolucent brown tumors, mobility) and the calcium regulators (PTH, vitamin D, calcitonin)
Acromegaly's growing jaw (Class I to Class III, diastemas, macroglossia); growth plates fused by the sex hormones, and implant timing
The three hormone classes with examples, receptors, and endocrine versus nervous signaling
Diabetes: type 1 versus type 2 (insulin ineffective, not deficient), oral manifestations and the sugar in saliva, the two-way periodontal link, SGLT2 drugs and UTIs
Hyperthyroid versus hypothyroid dental considerations (hypothyroidism far more common), and the recurrent laryngeal nerve in thyroid surgery
Sex hormones and the mouth: puberty, pregnancy gingivitis and the interproximal pyogenic granuloma, menopause
Pituitary hormones (ADH and diabetes insipidus), alpha and beta cells, and the adrenal medulla

hCG rescues the corpus luteum: made by the trophoblasts, it keeps the corpus luteum making progesterone (the hormone that readies the endometrium) and estrogen through the first trimester, LH and FSH stay suppressed, and it is what a pregnancy test measures

Prolactin versus oxytocin: prolactin makes the milk and oxytocin lets it down through the myoepithelial cells; during pregnancy progesterone antagonizes prolactin, so full milk production waits for delivery
Suckling's neuroendocrine effects: dopamine tonically inhibits prolactin; suckling lowers dopamine and raises oxytocin from the posterior pituitary; prolactin inhibits GnRH, so periods stop

Delivery and after: the estrogen-to-progesterone ratio rises; uterine distention, prostaglandins (PGF2 alpha for contraction, PGE2 for the cervix) and oxytocin from the posterior pituitary drive labor; oxytocin limits bleeding after delivery

The placenta takes over the steroids: estriol is the estrogen of pregnancy; the placenta makes progesterone on its own but needs the fetal adrenal's 17,20 desmolase and the fetal liver before its aromatase makes estriol
Human placental lactogen opposes insulin: an insulin-resistant, hyperinsulinemic pregnancy and gestational diabetes
What the placenta makes: hCG, hPL, relaxin, progesterone and estriol, but not oxytocin
Building the breast for milk: estrogen grows and branches the ducts, progesterone adds the alveoli, prolactin and cortisol raise the milk enzymes
The endocrine basis of contraception: the pill blunts the LH surge, progestin thickens the cervical mucus, high-dose estrogen prevents implantation
Fertilization: ZP3 sets off the acrosomal reaction, the sperm then binds ZP2, the oocyte finishes its second meiotic division, and the cortical reaction blocks polyspermy
Implantation at the blastocyst stage: trophoblasts, cytotrophoblasts (nurse cells) versus syncytiotrophoblasts (invasion)

GnRH analogs: the body releases GnRH in pulses, but a long-acting analog (goserelin, leuprolide) stimulates the pituitary continuously until it switches off LH, FSH and testosterone; mainly prostate cancer; anti-sex-hormone side effects

Blocking androgen metabolism and receptors: the 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors finasteride and dutasteride (Proscar and Propecia are one drug; his finasteride dental case) and the receptor antagonists flutamide and bicalutamide

How hormonal contraceptives prevent pregnancy: progestins activate the progestin receptor and suppress FSH and LH, so no ovulation; ethinyl estradiol in the combined pill; progestin-only pills (levonorgestrel) when estrogen is ruled out

Thromboembolism, the estrogens' most serious side effect: more clotting factors and less antithrombin III; shared by the SERMs and aromatase inhibitors (his raloxifene dental case); any clot, even years ago, rules estrogen out
Testosterone's adverse effects and cautions: hepatotoxicity (the most important), virilization in women, feminization in men, lower HDL, and when to avoid it (BPH, pregnancy, breast cancer in men)
Emergency contraception: Plan B (levonorgestrel, 72 hours, no prescription) versus ulipristal (a progestin receptor antagonist, 5 days, prescription)
SERMs: tamoxifen (breast antagonist, uterine agonist, ER-positive tumors only), raloxifene for osteoporosis, clomiphene for ovulation
Aromatase inhibitors: anastrozole blocks testosterone's conversion to estradiol to treat breast cancer; hot flashes and thromboembolism; not before menopause
Testosterone's two fates: 5-alpha-reductase makes DHT, the active form, and aromatase makes estradiol (the tall, osteoporotic man without aromatase)
What estrogen does and its side effects: female maturation and the endometrium, HDL and triglycerides up, bone protected; progesterone added to protect the uterus
The estrogen drugs: estradiol from the ovary, ethinyl estradiol in oral contraceptives, and the indications
How the sex steroids act (nuclear receptors) and what testosterone does (red cells, water retention, muscle); testosterone cypionate, the depot; progesterone matures the endometrium

Recognizing the blood cells and their jobs: red cells (most of the cells) carry oxygen and carbon dioxide, platelets come from megakaryocytes ("just knowledge you should know") and start clotting, and the white cells come in two classes and five types: the granulocytes and the agranulocytes (monocytes and lymphocytes), each with its share, most to least common, its nucleus and its line in the hematopoiesis tree

The white cells' jobs: the neutrophil (multi-lobed, the first line of defense against bacteria), eosinophil (red granules, major basic protein against parasites, allergy), basophil (dark blue granules, heparin, asthma) and monocyte (becomes the macrophage)

B and T cells: a B cell whose antibody fits an antigen recruits helper T cells and becomes a plasma cell that releases that antibody, in a secondary organ; helper T cells help the B cells, cytotoxic T cells kill what they bind, and T cells carry memory

NK cells: no B or T markers and no specific receptors; MHC class I on a healthy cell binds the inhibitory receptor and stops the killing, a cell missing it is killed, and too many activating ligands cause induced killing; in ADCC, CD16 binds IgG's constant region

Innate versus adaptive immunity: what the body just does (barriers, low pH, lysozyme, thiocyanate, interferons, phagocytes, NK cells), versus the antibodies of the humoral arm ("think B-cell response") and the T cells of the cellular arm

Primary versus secondary lymphoid organs: the primary ones are just the bone marrow and the thymus (not GALT), where B and T cells become immunocompetent without antigen ("bone marrow, B cells, thymus, T cells"); every other one, lymph nodes, MALT and GALT, and the spleen, is secondary
The spleen: the PALS, the T cell sheath around the central artery ("associate this PALS with the spleen"); white pulp and red pulp; and what the spleen does

The thymus: epithelioreticular cells form its stroma ("I do want you to know that"), reticular cells everywhere else; the dense, dark cortex versus the lighter medulla; and involution to fat by the teens

The lymph node: the lymph's route (afferent lymphatic, subcapsular sinus, trabecular sinuses, efferent lymphatic); activation in the paracortex and follicles, B cells multiplying in germinal centers and plasma cells secreting antibody in the medulla

T cell education: precursors in through postcapillary venules, out to the cortex, positive and negative selection, single CD4 or CD8 cells out to the secondary organs, and 95 to 99 percent selected out by apoptosis
Classifying the leukemias on two axes: acute (blasts that don't mature) or chronic (cells that still mature), and myeloid or lymphoid: AML, ALL, CML and CLL

Acute versus chronic leukemia (onset, course, blasts, platelets, organomegaly) and leukemia's clinical consequences: marrow failure (anemia, bleeding, infection) and cells growing in tissues (bone pain, spleen, liver, nodes, and the gums, where a dentist may be the first clue)

Hodgkin versus non-Hodgkin: Hodgkin is usually localized, spreads contiguously, rarely leaves the nodes and never involves the blood, with a few large Reed-Sternberg cells; non-Hodgkin lymphoma is usually widespread, can skip node groups, often starts outside the nodes, can reach the blood, and is mostly B-cell
AML's diagnostic threshold (more than 20 percent blasts), Auer rods (a myeloid blast, never ALL), and AML in adults versus ALL in children
ALL, the acute leukemia of young children (usually 1 to 5 years old, a poor prognosis under 1): B-ALL most often, and T-ALL, confirmed as T-cell by testing rather than by its look
Chronic myeloid leukemia, the chronic leukemia he said to know: BCR-ABL1 and the Philadelphia chromosome, a very high count with every stage of maturation and few blasts, imatinib

CLL/SLL: one disease of small, mature B cells, named by where it is (blood or node); soccer-ball chromatin and smudge cells; at least 5 times 10 to the 9th B cells per liter for CLL; older patients, infections, largely incurable
Burkitt lymphoma: very aggressive and very fast-growing, t(8;14) and MYC, the starry sky of macrophages eating debris, the jaw, EBV, and excellent survival with chemotherapy
Mantle cell lymphoma: from the follicle's mantle zone, t(11;14) (nothing else among the lymphomas carries it), the cyclin D1 stain, older adults with enlarged nodes, survival much longer than it was

Mycosis fungoides, the most common skin lymphoma, an indolent T-cell lymphoma (patches, then plaques, then tumors), and Sézary syndrome, its aggressive form (erythroderma, nodes and cerebriform Sézary cells in the blood)

The other B-cell lymphomas and their associations: follicular lymphoma's t(14;18) and BCL2, diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (about 30 percent of adult lymphomas), and marginal zone (MALT) lymphoma, the one dentists will see most, with its infections and autoimmune links

The two acute leukemias he said you need: acute promyelocytic leukemia (t(15;17) PML-RARA, maturation stopped at the promyelocyte, DIC, cured by all-trans retinoic acid with arsenic trioxide) and acute monocytic leukemia, which can show in the gums
Peripheral T-cell lymphoma, only the gist he gave: very aggressive, B symptoms, a poor response to chemotherapy
Lymphoma categories, his closing point: which lymphomas are B-cell and which T-cell, which are indolent and which aggressive, and the part of the follicle each B-cell lymphoma comes from
The B symptoms, his "high-yield clues" (a fever of 38 °C or more, drenching night sweats, losing 10 percent of body weight in 6 months): they raise the suspicion, and the tissue makes the diagnosis

Cryptorchidism, a testis hidden outside the scrotum: the testes descend from the retroperitoneum through the inguinal canal; body heat halts spermatogenesis, so infertility and testicular cancer; surgery if it hasn't come down by the second year prevents the infertility, but the cancer risk stays

The categories of testicular tumors: 95 percent are germ cell tumors, from the spermatogonia, cured in more than 95 percent; the rest are sex cord-stromal tumors (Sertoli and Leydig cells) or mixed, with lymphoma (secondary) and metastases in older men

Seminoma versus the non-seminomatous germ cell tumors: seminoma is the most frequent, in young adults, white and solid without hemorrhage or necrosis, tied to cryptorchidism, usually without a serum marker, and radiosensitive; embryonal carcinoma, yolk sac tumor, choriocarcinoma and teratoma are more aggressive and don't respond as well

Prostatic adenocarcinoma and Gleason grading: the most frequent cancer in men, over 65, in the peripheral zone (no early obstruction), found by serum PSA, with osteoblastic bone metastases; Gleason runs from well-differentiated glands to masses and single cells, and worse is worse

Benign prostatic hyperplasia: hyperplasia of the glands and stroma around the urethra (the transition zone), in nearly every man after 50, which obstructs the urine; hormones play a role, and surgery treats severe obstruction

The common infections of the male tract: the glans and foreskin (nonspecific bacterial, or syphilis, gonorrhea and chlamydia), epididymitis (gonorrhea and chlamydia in young, sexually active men), and orchitis, which is uncommon (mumps, syphilis, tuberculosis, brucellosis)

HPV and the penis, the lecture's "remember": types 6 and 11 cause condyloma acuminatum, benign and verrucous; types 16 and 18 cause penile intraepithelial neoplasia, flat and red, about 30 percent invasive if untreated
Phimosis predisposes to carcinoma of the penis, the closing review: a foreskin that can't retract fills with smegma, then infection, chronic inflammation and carcinoma

Urothelial carcinoma: 90 percent of urinary tract tumors, most in the bladder, in adult men, with minimal painless hematuria; smoking is the strongest risk (four times, and quitting doesn't lower it), with dyes, pelvic radiation, cyclophosphamide and catheters
The two emergencies of the testis: torsion (a twisted spermatic cord, intensely painful; the testis infarcts) and inguinal hernia (bowel trapped in an open inguinal canal can infarct)

HPV and cervical neoplasia: cancer arises in the transformation zone, where the glandular and squamous epithelia "fight" and stay inflamed and open to HPV; the precursors are squamous intraepithelial lesions, low grade (CIN1, can regress) or high grade (CIN2 and CIN3, progress), about 90 percent HPV-linked (and more than 90 percent of cervical cancers), marked by the koilocyte

Lichen sclerosus, where the lecture paused "because this is important": an atrophic epithelium over dermal sclerosis and hyalinization, a parchment-like vulva; the non-infectious inflammatory disorder the lecture said leads to carcinoma, the HPV-independent vulvar squamous cell carcinoma of older women (her slide lists lichen planus beside it)

Infectious vaginitis: Candida (pseudohyphae, little sticks, a lot of inflammation) and Trichomonas vaginalis (a sexually transmitted protozoan that looks like a squamous cell with prolongations), against non-infectious atrophic vaginitis in older women
Condyloma acuminatum: HPV 6 and 11, the low-risk types; benign, finger-like and wart-like, with koilocytes, anywhere on the anogenital tract

The age patterns of the tumors: sarcoma botryoides (embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma) in girls under 5, with a good prognosis if treated in time; squamous cell carcinomas in women of reproductive age; the HPV-independent vulvar carcinoma and the aggressive serous and clear cell endometrial carcinomas in older women (70 to 80 on the slide)

The common disorders of the vulva, and neoplastic versus non-neoplastic: lichen simplex chronicus (thickened, leathery, from scratching), lichen sclerosus and lichen planus are inflammatory; squamous intraepithelial lesions, VaIN, squamous cell carcinoma, clear cell adenocarcinoma and sarcoma botryoides are neoplastic
Lichen planus, "because you're going to be dentists": vulvar and oral erosions together, with a white, lace-like pattern; a fresh biopsy (not formalin) for immunofluorescence; steroids
Preventing cervical cancer: less common in the United States thanks to Pap screening, the HPV vaccine (decades to show its full benefit), and management now based on each patient's risk

The two endometrial carcinomas, "just know": endometrioid adenocarcinoma (estrogen excess, obesity, estrogen without progesterone; well differentiated, less aggressive, younger women) and the aggressive serous and clear cell carcinomas of women over 65 (70 to 80 on the slide), not hormone-related
Breast carcinoma: DCIS needs treatment, LCIS is now considered benign; Paget disease of the nipple means a carcinoma underneath; the estrogen and progesterone receptors and HER2 guide the treatment
Chronic endometritis: plasma cells in the endometrial stroma, a common cause of infertility, treated with antibiotics
The ovary: most ovarian tumors are epithelial, from the surface, and ovarian cancer is aggressive and lethal
